## Why go beyond the dashboard?

<!-- EXAMPLE NEEDED: one real request where a dashboard wasn't enough (e.g., someone looked at the dashboard and still asked "so what does this mean?"). Say it in the notes. -->

Dashboards expanded access to data, but access isn't understanding.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.compare-card .before .fragment}
**Dashboards**

- Show the numbers and filters
- Built for open-ended exploration
- Leave interpretation to the viewer
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.compare-card .after .fragment}
**Reports that tell the story**

- Add context and meaning
- Built for specific decisions/committees
- Point to a takeaway and next step
:::
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Talk about how dashboards are great for exploration but don't tell the story. Reports are still needed to interpret the data and point to action.

This is esp important in the age of AI, where numbers can be spat out quickly, but interpretation and context are still needed to make sense of them, and that's where we come in.
:::

## Consistent visualizations: one function, every chart

Create a function to make the same style figures for all predictors to outcomes.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="30%"}
- Branding, colors, fonts
- Clean layout (gridlines, values)
- Legend
- Readable labels
- Warnings
- Export sizes
:::

::: {.column width="70%"}
::::: {.code-scroll}
::: {.code-label}
**1. Wide → long → summarize:** works for any number of groups [(lines 132–150)]{.lines}
:::

```{.r code-line-numbers="false"}
summarise_outcomes <- function(data, student_groups, outcomes,
                               by = c("College", "year"),
                               digits = 0) {
  data %>%
    pivot_longer(all_of(student_groups),
                 names_to = "Student_Group",
                 values_to = "in_group") %>%
    filter(in_group == 1) %>%
    pivot_longer(all_of(outcomes),
                 names_to = "Outcome",
                 values_to = "has_outcome") %>%
    group_by(across(all_of(by)), Student_Group, Outcome) %>%
    summarise(total = sum(!is.na(has_outcome)),
              n = sum(has_outcome == 1, na.rm = TRUE),
              pct = round(100 * n / total, digits),
              .groups = "drop")
}
```

::: {.code-label}
**2. IVC + State in one table** [(lines 237–239)]{.lines}
:::

```{.r code-line-numbers="false"}
summary_long <-
  summarise_outcomes(ivc, student_groups, outcomes) %>%
  bind_rows(statewide) %>%
  mutate(Source = paste(College, year))
```

::: {.code-label}
**3. The plot core:** one bar per source, one panel per outcome [(inside make_comparison_plot)]{.lines}
:::

```{.r code-line-numbers="false"}
ggplot(plot_data,
       aes(x = Group_Label, y = pct, fill = Source)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.72),
           width = 0.64) +
  geom_text(aes(label = bar_label, color = low_n,
                group = Source),
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.72),
            vjust = -0.25) +
  facet_wrap(~ Outcome, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = fill_colors)
# ... theme settings
```

::: {.code-label}
**4. Every group x outcome combination in one loop** instead of 12 copy-pasted calls [(lines 270–277)]{.lines}
:::

```{.r code-line-numbers="false"}
plot_grid <- expand_grid(group_set = names(group_sets),
                         outcome = outcomes)

group_plots <- pmap(plot_grid, function(group_set, outcome) {
  build_plot(group_sets[[group_set]], outcome,
             size = plot_sizes[[group_set]] %||%
               plot_sizes$default)
})
```
:::::
:::
::::

build the template once, then use it for multiple reports

## A reproducible workflow (between reports)

::::: {.flow .detail}
::: {.step .manual}
Where I started: copy `setup.R`

Paste it into each new report, then manually delete/add what's relevant.

**Examples:** libraries, functions, themes
:::
::: {.step .fragment fragment-index=1}
Where I am now: an R package

Package calls report templates, functions, and themes.

One version, loaded everywhere with `library()`.

**Examples:** `use_report(format = "pdf")`, `use_presentation()`, `+ theme_fc()`
:::
:::::


::: {.notes}
Vinnie · ~45 sec · 30:15
- I used to copy setup.R into every new report and delete what didn't apply. Every report drifted a little.
- Now it's an R package: one version of the templates, functions, and themes, loaded with library().
- New report? One line, and it's already branded.
:::

## Example toolkit: R

::::: {.columns .toolkit-split}
:::: {.column width="34%"}
::: {.card}
[R]{.card-title}
*the analyses of the report*

- Data cleaning and analyses
- Reusable chart functions
- Create a package or reusable file
:::
::::

:::: {.column width="66%"}
::: {.code-scroll .wrap}
::: {.code-label}
**setup.R**
:::

```{.r code-line-numbers="false"}
# ---- Libraries ----
library(tidyverse) # data wrangling/viz
library(plotly) # cool charts
library(here) # file paths
library(readxl) # Excel import
library(writexl) # Excel export
library(haven) # SPSS/SAS/Stata import
library(glue) # Flexible text interpolation
library(flextable) # pretty tables
library(ggtext) # rich text in ggplot (HTML/Markdown)
library(ragg) # raster rendering for plots
library(extrafont) # font management
library(htmltools) # html in reports
library(quarto) #render quarto from R

loadfonts(device = "win", quiet = TRUE)

# ---- Fullerton College Color Palette ----
fc_colors <- c(
  "Blue" = "#0F406B",
  "Yellow" = "#FFD600",
  "Sky" = "#375E9E",
  "Creek" = "#5DCCD4",
  "Breeze" = "#BAEEED",
  "LemonZest" = "#F5F3BF",
  "Rustic" = "#E6605B",
  "Elderberry" = "#1B0D42"
)

# Neutral tone for text, lines, etc.
fc_blue <- "#0F406B"
fc_gray <- "#333333"

# ---- FC ggplot Theme ----
theme_fc <- function(base_size = 12, base_family = "Century Gothic") {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size, base_family = base_family) +
    theme(
      text = element_text(family = base_family, color = fc_gray),
      plot.title = element_text(
        face = "bold",
        color = fc_colors["Blue"],
        size = rel(1.2),
        hjust = 0.5
      ),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(color = fc_gray, hjust = 0.5),
      axis.title = element_text(color = fc_gray, face = "bold"),
      axis.text = element_text(color = fc_gray),
      panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#DDDDDD"),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      plot.caption = element_text(color = fc_gray, size = rel(0.9), hjust = 1),
      legend.title = element_text(color = fc_gray, face = "bold"),
      legend.text = element_text(color = fc_gray),
      plot.margin = margin(10, 10, 10, 10)
    )
}


# Color and fill scales for ggplot2 using the FC color palette

scale_fill_fc <- function(..., discrete = TRUE) {
  if (discrete) {
    scale_fill_manual(values = rep(unname(fc_colors), length.out = 20), ...)
  } else {
    scale_fill_gradientn(colours = unname(fc_colors), ...)
  }
}

scale_color_fc <- function(..., discrete = TRUE) {
  if (discrete) {
    scale_color_manual(values = rep(unname(fc_colors), length.out = 20), ...)
  } else {
    scale_color_gradientn(colours = unname(fc_colors), ...)
  }
}

# Set as default ggplot theme, yay!
theme_set(theme_fc())

```
:::
::::
:::::

::: {.notes}
Vinnie · ~45 sec · 32:15
- Three tools, three jobs. R does the analysis.
- Scroll the setup file: libraries, the college palette, one ggplot theme. theme_set() at the end means every chart is on-brand by default.
:::

```{.css code-line-numbers="false"}
h1, h2, h3, h4 {
  font-family: var(--font-body);
  color: var(--fc-blue);
  font-weight: 700;
  margin-top: 1em;
  margin-bottom: 0.5em;

  padding-bottom: 4px;

  padding-inline-start: var(--space-sm);

  font-weight: 600;
}

/* Subtitle (below report title) */
#subtitle {
  font-family: var(--font-body);
  font-size: var(--subtitle-size);
  font-weight: 700;
  color: var(--fc-gray);
  letter-spacing: 0.5px;
  margin: 10px 0 32px;
  border: none !important;
}
```

## Scaling reports: parameterized reporting

Project example: Individualized Faculty Course Success Reports

- Professional Learning Committee recommended, Faculty Senate supported: an individualized course success report for **every faculty member**, every year
  - Disaggregated course success rates and drop reasons
  - Emailed as a PDF, with guiding questions for reflection
  - A tool for professional learning, not evaluation
  - Power BI dashboard later for further exploration

::::: {.tile-grid .cols-2 .fragment}
::: {.tile}
**860** reports in 2024–25
:::
::: {.tile}
**971** reports in 2025–26
:::
:::::

::: {.notes}
Vinnie · ~45 sec · 34:30
- Here's what all of that makes possible.
- The request: every faculty member gets their own course success report, every year, by email, with guiding questions.
- Stress that it's for professional learning, not evaluation. That framing is why faculty engage with it.
- Click: 860 reports last year, 971 this year. Nobody builds that many by hand.
:::

## Why parameterized reports?

::::: {.card-grid .compact}
::: {.card .fragment}
### Scalable

- One template, one loop
- A report for every person
:::
::: {.card .fragment}
### Individualized

- Sentences written from each person's data
- E.g., "12.1 points **above** the ISS"
:::
::: {.card .fragment}
### Better aesthetics

- Page breaks, figure numbers, branding
- Long tables flow onto the next page
:::
::: {.card .fragment}
### Rule-based using code

- Combine small groups
- Skip empty sections
:::
:::::

::: {.takeaway .fragment}
Dashboards are still useful for **exploration**. 
Parameterized reports are great for supplemental **individualized insights**.
:::

::: {.notes}
Vinnie · ~45 sec · 35:15
- Takeaway: dashboards aren't going away. This complements them.

:::

## Parameterized reporting steps

::::: {.flow .detail}
::: {.step}
**1. SQL pull**

One query for the year: every course, student, and faculty member.

Update the terms, save as CSV.
:::
::: {.step}
**2. Shared functions**

One R file that builds every stat, chart, and sentence.

Written once, used by every report.
:::
::: {.step}
**3. One template**

A .qmd with a `faculty_id` parameter.

Filters all content to one person.
:::
::: {.step}
**4. Render loop**

Runs the template once per faculty ID.

~30 sec each; logs every render.
:::
::: {.step}
**5. Automated email**

Sends each PDF to its owner in batches.

Logged, so no one gets it twice and to check bouncebacks.
:::
:::::

::: {.notes}
Vinnie · ~1:00 · 36:00
- Left to right, about 10 seconds each.
- The only yearly changes: the terms in the SQL and the academic year.
- Steps 2 to 5 run unattended. Rendering is ~30 sec per report, so the full run is a few hours in the background.
- The send log is what keeps anyone from getting two emails.
:::

## Parameterized reporting: the key idea

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.code-label}
**1. Template** (faculty_template.qmd): declare a parameter
:::

```{.yaml code-line-numbers="false"}
---
title: "Course Success Report"
format: pdf
params:
  faculty_id: null   # filled in by the loop
---
```

::: {.code-label}
**2. Template**: every stat, chart, and sentence uses it
:::

```{.r code-line-numbers="false"}
summarize_overall_success(
  df,
  faculty_id_val = params$faculty_id
)
```
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
::: {.code-label}
**3. Script** (render_all_faculty.R): render once per ID
:::

```{.r code-line-numbers="false"}
for (fid in faculty_ids) {
  quarto_render(
    input = "faculty_template.qmd",
    execute_params = list(faculty_id = fid),
    output_file = paste0(
      "Course_Success_2025-26_", fid, ".pdf"
    )
  )
}
```


:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Vinnie · ~1:00 · 37:00
:::

## Parameterized reporting: lessons learned

::::: {.card-grid .compact}
::: {.card .fragment}
### By the numbers

- ~30 seconds per report
- Runs unattended
- Each faculty member gets **only their own** report
:::
::: {.card .fragment}
### Next year

- Change the terms and academic year
- Re-run
- Same design, comparable year to year
:::
::: {.card .fragment}
### What helped

- Log every render and send
- No double emails, easy restarts
- Write directions for future you
:::
:::::

::: {.takeaway .fragment}
The dashboard is for **exploring**. The report is for **reflecting**.
:::

::: {.notes}
Vinnie · ~45 sec · 39:00
:::

## What to automate, and what not to

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.compare-card .after}
**Automate**

- Recurring cleaning steps
- Charts for every group
- Branding and formatting
- One report to be customized as needed

::: {.ai-note .fragment fragment-index=1}
**AI can help:** debugging code, alt text, contrast checks
:::
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.compare-card .before}
**Don't automate**

- What the results mean
- Campus context and history
- Small-sample judgment calls
- Recommendations and conclusions

::: {.ai-note .fragment fragment-index=1}
**AI isn't perfect:** verifying code, checking alt text
:::
:::
:::
::::


::: {.notes}
Even if AI can help with repetitive tasks, 1) it isn't always correct and 2) it can't provide context or the framing you need for your specific audience.
:::
